title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In hardware, manufacturing is the price of admission, but distribution and cash conversion determine whether the enterprise survives.
epigraph.author: Manufacturing maxim

web_blocks.text: Kody Technolab’s go-to-market (GTM) architecture is organized around a dual-channel distribution model. Specifically, direct enterprise institutional sales across India, paired with specialized international value-added distributor (VAD) and joint venture networks in the Middle East and North America. In the domestic Indian market, the company sells directly to hospitality operators, corporate real estate developers, municipal bodies. Event organizers via dedicated technical sales teams based in Ahmedabad and Mumbai. In overseas markets—which contributed approximately 38% of FY26 revenue—Kody operates through strategic partnerships, most notably Falcon Tech Robotics LLC and Hypermedia FZ-LLC in Dubai for retail media deployment. Also, Platinum Group in Abu Dhabi for enterprise automation. This distributor-led model reduces overseas customer acquisition overhead. However, it introduces distributor payment cycles and extended shipping transit times. [1][3][8]

The company’s manufacturing, integration. Testing footprint is concentrated in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, located in the Electronic Estate / GIDC industrial cluster. The facility encompasses mechanical assembly lines, surface-mount technology (SMT) and PCB testing benches, cleanroom sensor calibration tracks, wire-harness routing stations. Final endurance testing obstacle courses where assembled robots undergo continuous 48-hour burn-in navigation trials. The production process is modular. Specifically, rather than casting and stamping raw metals in-house, Kody outsources heavy chassis fabrication and plastic shell molding to specialized domestic engineering vendors in Gujarat, focusing its internal workforce on embedded electronics integration, motor drive assembly, LiDAR/sensor calibration. Kody OS firmware installation. [2][4][5]

A granular analysis of the robotics bill of materials (BOM) reveals substantial exposure to global electronics and semiconductor supply chains. The primary imported sub-assemblies include solid-state LiDAR sensors (sourced from specialized global manufacturers), optical depth cameras (Intel RealSense or equivalent), high-performance compute modules (NVIDIA Jetson embedded AI boards). Brushless DC hub motors. Domestic Indian sourcing accounts for structural aluminum framing, wiring harnesses, sheet metal brackets, acrylic fairings. Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery pack assemblies. Gross margins on raw robotic hardware typically range between 45% and 52% on a pure bill-of-materials basis. However, because specialized sensors must be procured with cash advances or letters of credit from overseas suppliers, inventory turnover is inherently constrained. [2][4]

The commercial billing cycle is where Kody’s business model experiences acute working-capital friction. A standard commercial robotics engagement follows a four-stage milestone structure. Specifically, (1) 20% to 25% advance upon contract signing and design freeze. (2) 40% upon factory acceptance testing and dispatch. (3) 25% upon on-site delivery, floor mapping. Commissioning. And (4) a 10% to 15% retention fee payable after a 90-day defect liability period. Because institutional customers (shopping malls, corporate offices, municipal agencies) frequently delay site readiness or stretch commissioning sign-offs, trade receivables remain locked on the balance sheet for extended periods. As documented in the audited fundamentals, trade debtor days expanded from 177 days in FY25 to 192 days in FY26. This pushed total working capital days from 62 days to an alarming 197 days. [1][6]

web_blocks.takeaway: For every ₹100 of revenue, Kody generated ₹30.0 of operating profit before depreciation, but heavy working capital absorption restricted CFO to ₹15.0. After ₹81.25 of cash capex, Free Cash Flow was deeply negative at -₹66.25 per ₹100 of sales (-₹53.0 Cr absolute). [1][6]

web_blocks.text: The mathematical reconciliation of the ₹100 waterfall block above illustrates the central economic reality of Kody Technolab. On ₹80.00 crore of consolidated revenue in FY26, raw material consumption, subcontracting. Manufacturing expenses consumed ₹56.00 crore (70.0% of revenue). This left ₹24.00 crore in operating profit (30.0%). Depreciation absorbed ₹3.00 crore (3.75%) and interest expense consumed ₹2.00 crore (2.5%). Meanwhile, non-operating other income contributed ₹7.00 crore (8.75%). Profit before tax stood at ₹26.00 crore (32.5%). Provision for tax took ₹9.00 crore (11.25%), yielding audited net profit of ₹17.00 crore (21.25%). [1][6]

However, the conversion from reported net profit into operating cash was severely diluted by working capital. Operating cash flow stood at only ₹12.00 crore (15.0% of revenue or ₹15.00 per ₹100 of sales) due to an ₹18+ crore cash drain into trade receivables and inventory buffers. Meanwhile, the company executed ₹65.00 crore in cash capital expenditure (part of an ₹86.00 crore total investing cash outflow) to expand assembly capacity, acquire diagnostic tooling. Build demo fleet assets. Subtracting cash capex of ₹65.00 crore from CFO of ₹12.00 crore yields a staggering negative free cash flow of negative ₹53.00 crore (negative ₹66.25 per ₹100 of sales). This structural cash deficit explains why Kody was compelled to raise fresh equity and convert warrants during 2025–2026. [1][6]

In total, Kody’s unit-level gross margins are structurally attractive on paper, reflecting the premium commanded by intelligent autonomous systems over raw sheet metal. However, enterprise-level unit economics are constrained by the cash conversion cycle. Until customer milestone collections accelerate and debtor days compress from 192 days down toward industry-standard levels of 90 to 110 days, Kody's rapid revenue growth will continue to devour cash rather than distribute it to shareholders. [1][4][6]

book_paragraphs: Let you and I follow a single Kody robot from the parts bin to the customer's loading dock, because it is in the logistics and invoicing details that an investor discovers whether a business actually makes money. Suppose Kody receives a purchase order for five Odigo robots from an overseas retail agency. What happens next on the balance sheet?

First, before a single wheel turns, Kody's procurement team must commit hard cash. They must wire payments or open letters of credit for solid-state LiDAR sensors, precision optical cameras, and NVIDIA Jetson AI computing modules from global semiconductor distributors. These are not commodity screws you buy down the street in Ahmedabad; they are specialized, high-cost components with lead times stretching from six to twelve weeks. Next, domestic suppliers in Gujarat stamp the aluminum chassis, cast the fairings, and wind the wiring harnesses. Kody's assembly technicians in Gandhinagar mount the electronics, calibrate the multi-sensor navigation stack on indoor test tracks, flash Kody OS, and conduct a 48-hour continuous navigation burn-in. At this stage, Kody has absorbed substantial cash in raw materials and direct labor.

Now consider the payment cycle. The customer typically pays a 20% down payment. Another 40% is invoiced when the robots pass factory inspection and ship. But then comes the real-world friction: shipping to the destination port, customs clearance, transit to the shopping mall, and on-site integration with the mall's local Wi-Fi and floor maps. The customer will not sign off on final commissioning—which unlocks the remaining 40% of the invoice—until the robots have operated flawlessly on the mall concourse for several weeks without incident. If the mall is undergoing renovations or delays IT integration, Kody’s invoice sits unpaid in accounts receivable.

This is why Kody's debtor days stood at an eye-watering 192 days in FY26. Think about what that number means: on average, it takes Kody more than six full months from the day it recognizes a sale to actually collect the cash in its bank account! Meanwhile, total working capital days expanded from 62 days in FY25 to 197 days in FY26. In an asset-light software business, a receivable delay is an annoyance. In a hardware manufacturing business with physical suppliers demanding prompt payment, a six-month collection delay is a cash-devouring monster.

The FY26 waterfall block we constructed above lays this bare with absolute arithmetic clarity. On every ₹100 of revenue that Kody booked in FY26, it spent ₹70 on materials and operational overhead, leaving ₹30 in operating profit. That sounds healthy enough. But when you look at the cash statement, operating cash flow was only ₹15 per ₹100 of sales, because the rest of the profit was trapped in customer receivables and inventory. Then look at capital expenditure: Kody spent ₹81.25 per ₹100 of sales building out its Gandhinagar plant, buying diagnostic test rigs, and building demonstrator fleets. The net result? For every ₹100 of revenue brought in the front door, ₹66.25 in cash flowed out the back door!

In total, Kody generated negative ₹53 crore in free cash flow in FY26. That is why the company had to issue warrants and raise equity capital. As you and I evaluate this business, we must never confuse accounting revenue with investable cash. Kody is building impressive machines, but right now, its customers are financing their automation on Kody's balance sheet.

To truly understand why Kody's working capital has exploded, you and I must examine the friction points embedded in international distributor agreements. When Kody sells an Odigo robot to an enterprise buyer in Dubai through its partner Falcon Tech or Hypermedia, the commercial journey is long and complex. First, components must be assembled and tested in Gandhinagar. Once the robot clears factory acceptance testing, it is crated, loaded into a shipping container, and transported by road to the port of Mundra or Nhava Sheva. Ocean freight across the Arabian Sea takes several weeks, followed by customs clearance and regulatory inspections at the port of Jebel Ali.

Upon arrival in Dubai, the robots do not immediately generate revenue. They must be transported to the customer’s site, unboxed, inspected for transit damage, connected to local cellular or Wi-Fi data networks, and integrated into the mall or exhibition facility’s local mapping system. Only after field engineers have completed dynamic calibration and the client’s operations team has verified autonomous operation over several days will the commercial commissioning certificate be signed. If the overseas client’s site preparation is delayed, or if municipal permits for robotic operation take longer than expected, Kody’s invoice remains frozen in uncollected receivables.

Meanwhile, consider the cash demands of Kody’s upstream supply chain. Specialized sensor manufacturers and semiconductor distributors do not offer 180-day credit terms to small Indian technology assemblers. If Kody wants to procure solid-state LiDAR sensors, NVIDIA Jetson computing boards, or high-precision depth cameras, it must pay cash upfront or open irrevocable letters of credit with commercial banks. The company is caught in a classic working-capital vice: cash flows out immediately to pay overseas component suppliers, while cash from downstream customers trickles in six to nine months later.

This dynamic explains why Kody's trade debtor days rose relentlessly from 103 days at the time of its IPO to 163 days in FY24, 177 days in FY25, and reached 192 days in FY26. Total working capital days surged from 62 days to an astonishing 197 days. Think of what this means in practical business terms: for every single rupee of sales that Kody books on its income statement, more than half a rupee sits locked up in unpaid customer bills and inventory buffers for over six months! A business model structured like this cannot fund its own growth; the faster it expands, the more cash it absorbs, and the more reliant it becomes on external equity capital.

Consider also the customer psychology in early-stage commercial robotics adoption. When a hotel chain or a retail mall operator signs a purchase order for five autonomous robots, they are not simply buying a piece of machinery; they are disrupting their established operational workflow. Front-of-house staff must be retrained, kitchen expediters must learn a new dispatch interface, and facility managers must establish daily cleaning and maintenance routines for charging docks. If early pilots encounter minor glitches—a robot pausing because of sunlight glare on a reflective marble floor, or a Wi-Fi dead zone in a basement service corridor—client managers hesitate to sign off on final acceptance certificates. These operational growing pains are completely normal in robotics deployments, but they introduce commercial friction that directly inflates accounts receivable days on Kody's balance sheet.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A gross margin of 50% on bill of materials is an illusion if it takes 192 days to collect the invoice while assembly capex runs at 80% of revenue. The true test of Kody's distribution engine is not how many robots it can ship to overseas exhibition booths, but how quickly those exhibition deployments convert into unconditional cash in the bank.
